hints.title: Replace both partial sums
hints.body: Use Sn=n[2a+(n−1)d]2. In the inequality S8>3S6, the factor 3 multiplies the entire six-term sum.
hints.recap: Translate the sums before reasoning about signs.

recall.reminder: Use exact AP block sizes and endpoints when combining partial sums.

hints.title: Simplify the joint restriction
hints.recap: The restriction is on a weighted sum, not two individual signs.
hints.pitfall: A negative sum does not force each term to be negative.
hints.pause: Can a positive a be offset by a sufficiently negative <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>?

hints.title: Construct opposing sign examples
hints.body: First fix a=1 and choose a permitted d; then fix d=1 and choose a permitted a.
hints.recap: A forced sign must hold for every permitted pair.
hints.pitfall: Check the examples in the original sum inequality.
hints.pause: Use the completed examples to decide which individual signs are determined.

recall.reminder: A forced sign must hold for every permitted pair.

solution:
S8=4(2a+7d) and S6=3(2a+5d). Therefore

S8>3S6 ⇔ 8a+28d>18a+45d ⇔ 10a+17d<0.

For (a, d)=(1, −1), the left side of the final inequality is −7, so a may be positive and d negative. For (a, d)=(−2, 1), it is −3, so a may be negative and d positive. Both examples satisfy the original sum inequality.

Consequently neither a nor d has an individually determined sign.

Answer F.
knowledgePattern: Translate an arithmetic-sum inequality without overclaiming individual signs
